description:
Long ago, we sent machines to explore the Moon, Mars and deep space. They took pictures, dug up rocks and taught us amazing things. Then one by one, they went quiet.
Some sit in the dust. Some are still traveling, far from home. None of them is forgotten.
We are astronomy students, and we're here to tell their story: what they did, what they learned, and why they still matter.
summary:
"Abandoned but Not Forgotten"
is a 77-page illustrated storybook about 24 real robotic missions to the Moon, Mars and deep space, narrated in three parts by the Moon, Mars and "the Dark" between the stars. Each chapter has a Mission Card, a story to read aloud, a Science Corner, a discussion question and NASA sources. We changed the challenge's question from "abandoned" to "kept": many of these machines were crashed on purpose or went silent, yet each left something behind, whether a photograph, a measurement, a discovery or a lesson, as Ranger 7's photos, Apollo 12's visit to Surveyor 3 and the Voyagers still travelling between stars show. Every fact comes from NASA, its centers such as JPL, or its mission partners. This matters because space science is often shared as numbers and press releases, while a story is easier to remember. School students get simple explanations and discussion questions, college readers get dates, figures and checkable links, and the engineers behind these missions are honoured. Made by six students from Pakistan, the book shows that space curiosity belongs to everyone.
details:
Project Details:

It is a digital storybook, a PDF, that teaches real space history through narrated stories. Each chapter combines a story, a fact card, a science idea, a reflection question and sources, so readers can enjoy it, learn from it and verify it.

It makes NASA mission history easy to read and remember. Students get a clear introduction to different types of spacecraft (flybys, orbiters, landers, rovers and impactors), and teachers can use the discussion questions in class.

We want readers to see old spacecraft as explorers worth remembering, not as failures or debris. We hope the book makes more students curious about space science and encourages them to check NASA's mission pages for themselves.

The research came from NASA and mission-partner websites. We used NASA, JPL-Caltech, Arizona State University, ISRO and Intuitive Machines photographs, plus our own illustrations. The PDF was produced with the ReportLab library (Python) and set in the Poppins and Liberation Serif fonts. No special hardware was needed; we worked on ordinary computers. We also used Capcut for making the video.

Instead of a plain list of missions, we gave a voice to the Moon, Mars and the Dark, so the book reads like a museum tour with no roof. The same chapter structure makes every mission easy to compare, and the report cards let readers see each part at a glance. The "kept" idea turns the sadness of "abandoned" into pride.

Factors considered:
Accuracy: every fact is sourced, and the creative voices are clearly separated from the facts.
Audience: the language is simple enough for school students but detailed enough for college readers.
Honesty: the book says it is a student project and not an official NASA publication, and it credits other agencies' missions properly.
Images and permissions: we credit image sources, and our own artwork is marked "made for this book".


Updates: we note that space science changes and that "still working" means as of our 2026 research.

Thank you!
